subject: physiology
title: Electroencephalography Waves and Non-REM Sleep Stages

steps.tx: Electrical activity recorded non-invasively from the human scalp reflects summed extracellular postsynaptic potentials generated by millions of vertically oriented cortical pyramidal neurons. These rhythmic potential oscillations represent **electroencephalography waves**, whose frequency and voltage vary dynamically in response to arousal, sleep stages, metabolic states, and underlying pathology.
steps.say: EEG waves represent summed postsynaptic potentials from cortical pyramidal cells, reflecting brain states.

vis.caption: Scalp electroencephalographic montages displaying synchronized epileptiform seizure discharge waves.
vis.alt: Continuous epileptiform seizure activity recorded on scalp electroencephalogram

steps.tx: In an awake adult relaxing quietly with eyes closed in an unstimulating environment, the electroencephalogram is dominated by rhythmic eight to thirteen hertz waveforms. Known as the **alpha rhythm**, these waves localize prominently over the occipital and parietal cortices, disappearing abruptly upon opening the eyes or engaging in mental calculation in a phenomenon termed alpha block.
steps.say: Alpha rhythm comprises eight to thirteen hertz waves recorded from occipital regions during relaxed wakefulness.

nodes.label: Subject Rests Awake in Dark Quiet Room with Closed Eyes
Thalamocortical Neurons Enter Synchronous Pacemaker Oscillation (8-13 Hz)
High-Amplitude Alpha Waves Dominate Occipital and Parietal Leads
Eye Opening Delivers Visual Stream That Desynchronizes Rhythm into Beta Waves

steps.tx: When an individual opens their eyes, focuses visual attention, or performs active cognitive work, synchronized alpha oscillations are replaced by low-voltage, high-frequency waveforms. These fast fourteen to thirty hertz oscillations represent **beta waves**, reflecting cortical desynchronization where independent functional neuronal circuits process distinct cognitive and sensory streams.
steps.say: Beta waves are fast fourteen to thirty hertz oscillations signaling focused cognitive processing and wakefulness.

left.title: Alpha Rhythm (8 to 13 Hz)
points: Moderate voltage amplitude (20 to 60 microvolts)
Prominent over posterior occipital and parietal scalp regions
Signifies relaxed, quiet, awake state with eyes closed
Readily abolished by sensory stimulation or mental attention (desynchronization)

right.title: Beta Activity (14 to 30 Hz)
points: Low voltage amplitude (typically under 20 microvolts)
Prominent over anterior frontal and central scalp regions
Signifies active cognitive vigilance, intense focus, or anxiety
Promoted by pharmacological central GABA-A agonists like benzodiazepines

steps.tx: Intermediate frequency oscillations spanning four to seven hertz appear normally during emotional stress in adults and during light drowsiness. Designated **theta waves**, they localize predominantly over the temporal and parietal lobes in children and young adults, but their focal persistence during full alert wakefulness in adults signals focal structural brain pathology.
steps.say: Theta waves are four to seven hertz waveforms seen in drowsiness, childhood, and emotional stress.

vis.caption: Abnormal high-voltage slow-wave cerebral rhythmic discharges illustrating cortical synchrony.
vis.alt: Focal and generalized high-voltage cortical discharges on electroencephalogram

steps.tx: The slowest and highest-amplitude physiological brain rhythms oscillate below three point five hertz with voltages exceeding seventy-five microvolts. Termed **delta waves**, these massive waveforms signify profound thalamocortical synchrony characteristic of deep stage three non-REM slow-wave sleep, severe metabolic encephalopathy, or surgical general anesthesia.
steps.say: Delta waves are slow, high-voltage rhythms under three point five hertz that dominate deep slow-wave sleep.

left.title: Theta Activity (4 to 7 Hz)
points: Moderate amplitude (30 to 50 microvolts)
Normal in infants, children, and during adult stage N1 drowsiness
Involved in hippocampal memory encoding and spatial navigation
Pathological when present focally over awake adult cortical lobes

right.title: Delta Activity (< 3.5 Hz)
points: High amplitude (often exceeding 75 to 100 microvolts)
Normal signature of stage N3 non-REM slow-wave deep sleep
Driven by intrinsic burst firing of hyperpolarized thalamic relay neurons
Indicates severe diffuse cortical injury, coma, or toxic encephalopathy

steps.tx: Sleep is divided physiologically into non-rapid eye movement and rapid eye movement categories. As wakefulness transitions into sleep, **stage N1 sleep** marks the initial light somnolence phase, where occipital alpha waves drop below fifty percent and are replaced by low-amplitude mixed-frequency theta activity and slow rolling eye movements.
steps.say: Stage N1 sleep is light transitional drowsiness where alpha waves give way to low-voltage theta rhythms.

nodes.label: Subject Drowses off, Exhibiting Slow Horizontal Rolling Eye Movements
Alpha Waves Diminish to Under 50% of the Epoch Duration
Replaced by Low-Amplitude, Mixed-Frequency Background (4-7 Hz Theta)
Vertex Sharp Waves Appear Centrally; Easily Aroused by Soft Stimuli

steps.tx: True physiological sleep onset is formalized by the appearance of distinctive electroencephalographic signatures defining stage N2 sleep. The hallmark features are **sleep spindles and K complexes**, generated by rhythmic reticular thalamic nucleus bursts that filter external environmental noises to safeguard the continuity of sleep.
steps.say: Stage N2 sleep is defined by sleep spindles and K complexes that protect sleep from external disturbances.

left.title: Sleep Spindles
points: Sinusoidal 11 to 16 Hz bursts lasting 0.5 to 1.5 seconds
Generated by GABAergic reticular thalamic nucleus pacemaker neurons
Attenuates sensory transmission through thalamus to protect sleep
Correlates with overnight memory consolidation and cognitive integration

right.title: K Complexes
points: Sharp negative high-voltage peak followed by slower positive wave
Duration exceeds 0.5 seconds, prominent across frontocentral midline
Evoked intrinsically or by subtle external auditory environmental clicks
Suppresses cortical information processing to prevent behavioral arousal

steps.tx: Progression into deep restorative rest constitutes stage N3, designated slow-wave sleep. Driven by synchronized hyperpolarisation of thalamocortical networks, slow **delta waves dominate stage N3 sleep** for at least twenty percent of epoch duration, during which heart rate, arterial blood pressure, and metabolic rate fall to basal 24-hour nadirs while growth hormone surges.
steps.say: Stage N3 slow-wave sleep features high-amplitude delta waves, low metabolic rate, and pituitary growth hormone release.
